candidates.attacker_control: A crafted link to the default endpoint `/oauth2/authorization/{registrationId}` controls the `action` request parameter (fully attacker-controlled; used verbatim as `{action}`). The `{baseUrl}` portion comes from the request URL (scheme, Host header / server name, port), which is attacker-influenced when a front proxy forwards an unvalidated Host/X-Forwarded-Host or when the app is reachable under alternate hostnames. The victim's browser is then redirected by the application to the authorization server with the attacker-influenced redirect_uri.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The `action` templating is documented/intended for distinguishing login vs authorize flows, and deriving {baseUrl} from the current request is the standard mechanism for multi-domain deployments (DefaultOAuth2AuthorizationRequestResolver Javadoc and expandRedirectUri comments). OAuth2 `state` is generated server-side (Base64StringKeyGenerator) and validated against the session-stored authorization request (OAuth2AuthorizationExchangeValidator lines 43-51), and the response URL is checked against the stored redirect URI (same validator line 48; OAuth2AuthorizationCodeGrantFilter.shouldProcessAuthorizationResponse lines 143-156) — so a naive cross-session login-CSRF/code-injection is blocked; the weakness is the redirect_uri value itself, not the state check. Most major providers strictly match registered redirect URIs, which limits real-world exploitability. The same {baseUrl} substitution pattern also exists in the reactive resolver, so if this is intended upstream behavior rather than the fixed defect, the finding is a hardening gap rather than a definite vulnerability.
candidates.impact: The application can be used as an open redirector and, if the authorization server accepts the influenced redirect_uri, the OAuth2 authorization code (and then the user's login/token) can be delivered to an attacker-chosen endpoint: authorization-code/token interception and account takeover, or at minimum a credible phishing/redirection primitive launched from the trusted application URL.
candidates.prerequisites: OAuth2 2.0 login/authorization-code flow enabled with the default `/oauth2/authorization/{registrationId}` endpoint; the client registration's redirect-URI template must contain the `{baseUrl}`/`{action}` placeholders (the default templates for CommonOAuth2Provider providers do) or a custom template that exposes them. Exploitation of the full code-redirection impact additionally requires the authorization server (or a malicious/attacker-registered client) to accept a redirect_uri that differs from a strictly registered value, and victim interaction (clicking the link / completing authorization).
candidates.root_cause: DefaultOAuth2AuthorizationRequestResolver.expandRedirectUri() computes the OAuth2 redirect_uri by substituting {baseUrl} from UrlUtils.buildFullRequestUrl(request) (request scheme/serverName/serverPort, i.e. Host header) and {action} from the unvalidated request parameter "action" (getAction(request, "login")) into the client registration's redirect-URI template, with no allow-list check; OAuth2AuthorizationRequestRedirectFilter then redirects the user agent to the resulting authorization-request URI. The reactive counterpart behaves the same for {baseUrl}. Consequently the redirect_uri that (a) is sent to the authorization server and (b) is later stored/compared as "the client's redirect URI" can be influenced by the requester.
candidates.title: OAuth2 client builds authorization-request redirect_uri from attacker-influenced request data (action parameter / Host-derived baseUrl), enabling open redirect and authorization-code redirection
candidates.trace: GET /oauth2/authorization/{registrationId}?action=<attacker-value> -> OAuth2AuthorizationRequestRedirectFilter.doFilterInternal (line 149) calls the resolver -> DefaultOAuth2AuthorizationRequestResolver.resolve(request) reads action via getAction (lines 87-93) -> expandRedirectUri (lines 141-158) builds {baseUrl} from UrlUtils.buildFullRequestUrl(request) (line 146) and expands clientRegistration.getRedirectUriTemplate() with attacker-influenced action (lines 152-157) -> OAuth2AuthorizationRequest.Builder.redirectUri(...) stores it and buildAuthorizationRequestUri() emits it as the `redirect_uri` query parameter -> filter line 198 performs sendRedirect to the authorization server URI -> the authorization server returns the code/error to that redirect_uri. On return, OAuth2AuthorizationExchangeValidator.validate (lines 43-51) / OAuth2AuthorizationCodeGrantFilter.shouldProcessAuthorizationResponse compare the response's redirect URI against this same stored value, so the stored (attacker-influenced) value is the trust anchor rather than the client's registered URI.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-verified (no build/test execution permitted): I did not demonstrate an authorization server accepting the influenced redirect_uri, nor Host-header control in a deployment. I could not confirm which upstream security fix corresponds to this snapshot, so I cannot assert this is the exact fixing-commit defect; the servlet/reactive resolvers and the redirect filter are indexed only as navigation candidates, not proven data flow. The comparison logic that consumes the redirect_uri (OAuth2AuthorizationExchangeValidator) was read directly but its full runtime path was not executed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-601 URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect'); related CWE-346 origin validation / OAuth2 authorization-code redirection

coverage_summary: Source scope: 1597 files, all present in the relation index (index status complete; no missing files, no hash mismatches); no binary-like files excluded; test sources are not part of the snapshot (list/search under */src/test returned nothing), and no build/test execution was performed. I inspected security-critical code across modules: core (authentication providers, access-decision voters, expression roots, user details/JDBC, jackson2 session deserialization whitelist), web servlet (firewall, request wrappers, CSRF, session/context persistence, remember-me, basic/digest/pre-auth/x509/switch-user, exception translation, saved request/request cache, redirect/login/logout handlers, matchers, header writers), web reactive (server CSRF, redirect strategies, request cache, basic/bearer converters), config (annotations, LoginPage configurer, ExpressionUrlAuthorizationConfigurer), oauth2-core/client/jose/resource-server (authorization request/response resolvers, login and code-grant filters, token response clients, OIDC validator, JWT decoders/validators/bearer resolver), crypto (password encoders, key generators, encryptors), ldap, cas, openid, acl/jdbc, messaging matchers, and samples/itest/build files. Relation-index facts and edges were used only for navigation and were verified against source text; they do not prove reachability or exploitability.
limitations: No code was executed; no build, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were run, so all statements are source-level only and no finding is runtime-confirmed.
Test sources are absent from the snapshot, so regression tests that would identify the intended fixing commit could not be inspected.

The relation index provides syntactic navigation candidates only (no complete control/data-flow, no runtime reachability); every cited edge was manually verified in source text but coverage is reading-based, not exhaustive line-by-line over all 1597 files.

I could not map this snapshot to a specific CVE/fixing commit from source alone; the candidate is a lead selected for the strongest security impact and source evidence, and may be intended upstream behavior rather than the exact defect this case targets.
Exploitability of the submitted candidate depends on deployment factors (proxy Host handling and authorization-server redirect_uri enforcement) that cannot be verified from the snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: RegexRequestMatcher compiles patterns without Pattern.DOTALL (web/.../util/matcher/RegexRequestMatcher.java:66-75,113), the pre-fix state of a later authorization-bypass CVE; authorization rules using a '.'-terminated regex would not match newline-bearing paths.
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness pattern, but it requires application-specific regex patterns and the snapshot predates the corresponding fix by years, so it does not fit this case's timeframe; not the strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: OIDC ID token validation omits `iss` and `nonce` checks (OidcTokenValidator.java:62-64,106-111, documented as TODO gh-4413/gh-4442), weakening issuer binding and replay protection.
rejected_leads.reason: Explicitly documented as unimplemented upstream functionality (not a hidden check removal); no concrete attacker-controlled path to a login/authorization bypass shown, and no clear fixing-commit match for this snapshot window.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter / DefaultLogoutPageGeneratingFilter render hidden inputs and context path without HTML escaping (renderHiddenInputs, lines 296-302 / 96-102, 71).
rejected_leads.reason: The values are server/config-generated (CSRF token is a UUID from HttpSessionCsrfTokenRepository or a server-set cookie); no demonstrated attacker-controlled input reaches these sinks in the default configuration.
Documented, explicitly opt-in behavior (targetUrlParameter must be configured); default handlers do not expose it, so it is a hardening/configuration concern rather than a repository vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: OAuth2 authorization request state/replay handling (HttpSessionOAuth2AuthorizationRequestRepository) and CSRF/session components (CsrfFilter, CsrfWebFilter, session fixation/concurrency strategies) reviewed and found consistent with their security contracts.
rejected_leads.reason: No defect identified after source inspection: state is session-scoped and validated, CSRF token comparison present, session strategies canonical.

rejected_leads.lead: SwitchUserFilter does not itself check the caller's switch authority before impersonating (attemptSwitchUser, lines 216-247).
rejected_leads.reason: Upstream behavior delegates that enforcement to the authorization layer on the switch-user URL; no in-filter bypass demonstrated without a misconfiguration.

summary: Reviewed the Spring Security snapshot (1597 files, all indexed; no test sources, no binaries). Version metadata (gradle.properties: version=5.2.0.BUILD-SNAPSHOT, springBootVersion=2.1.0.M4; gradle/dependency-management.gradle: springVersion=5.1.1.RELEASE; no 2019 copyright headers) places the tree in the Nov/Dec 2018 development line. I audited core authentication/authorization (DaoAuthenticationProvider, AbstractUserDetailsAuthenticationProvider, AffirmativeBased, WebExpressionVoter, ProviderManager paths), web filters (StrictHttpFirewall, RequestWrapper, DefaultHttpFirewall, CsrfFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter, SecurityContext/Session management, RememberMe, Digest/Basic/X509/PreAuth, SwitchUser), OAuth2 client/resource-server/JOSE flows, LDAP, CAS/OpenID, crypto, ACL/JDBC, and messaging matchers. Most code matches upstream expectations. The single strongest issue is in the OAuth2 client authorization-request path: the `redirect_uri` sent to the authorization server is built from attacker-influenced request data (the `action` query parameter and the request URL/Host-derived `{baseUrl}`) with no allow-list validation, and the filter then redirects the user agent to the provider using that URI — an open-redirect / authorization-code-redirection primitive. I submit it as a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
